summary: Describes a way for DHCP servers to tell clients that no IP address is on offer and that the client should not make up an address for itself. It was later updated by RFC 8925.

plainLanguage.summary: Some computers, when they cannot find a server to give them an address, invent one so they can still reach the other computers on the same cable. That is wrong on a network where an administrator wants those machines to have no address at all, and this document gives the administrator a way to say so.

how to stop ipv4 link-local addresses with dhcp
what is the dhcp auto-configure option
subtitle: A DHCP option that lets a network operator tell a client not to pick an address for itself.

tldr.problem: When a computer finds no DHCP server, many operating systems make one up so that they can still talk on the local network. That is helpful on an unmanaged network but wrong on a managed one, where the administrator wants the machine to have no address at all. The client cannot tell the two situations apart, because a DHCP server is required to ignore requests from hosts it does not know.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines DHCP option 116. A client adds it to its DHCPDISCOVER, and a server that wants auto-configuration switched off answers with an offer of the address 0x00000000 and the option set to DoNotAutoConfigure. The client then leaves itself with no address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2563 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8925, which adds a DHCPv4 option for hosts that prefer to run in IPv6-only mode and forgo an IPv4 address.

sections.title: The Problem with Picking an Address
sections.content:
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol provides a method by which site administrators may supply IP addresses and other network parameters to network devices. However, some operating environments are not centrally maintained, and operating systems must be able to handle this quickly and easily.

IPv6 accounts for this, allowing an IPv6 stack to assign itself a global address in the absence of any other mechanism for configuration. But operating system designers cannot wait for IPv6 support everywhere; they need to be able to assume they will have IPv4 addresses, so that they may communicate with one another even in the smallest networks.

The document looks at three types of network node: a node for which the site administrator will hand out configuration information, a node on a network segment for which there is no site administrator, and a node on a network segment that has a central site administrator who chooses not to hand out any configuration information to the node. The difference between the second and third cases is the client's behaviour. In one case the node may assign itself an IP address and have full connectivity with other nodes on the local wire; in the last case the node is not told what to do, and while it may assign itself a network address in the same way, this may not be what the central administrator wants.

The first scenario is handled by the current DHCP standard. However, the DHCP specification says servers must silently ignore requests from hosts they do not know, so DHCP clients are unable to determine whether they are on a subnet with no administration or with administration that is choosing not to hand out addresses. This document describes a method by which clients will be able to determine whether or not the network is being centrally administrated, allowing it to decide whether it should assign itself a link-local address.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of network. On one, nobody is in charge, so a computer that finds no server can make up an address and carry on. On the other, somebody is in charge and wants machines with no address until they are given one. The computer cannot tell these apart, because a server is supposed to ignore a request from a host it has never seen.

sections.title: The Auto-Configure Option
sections.content:
This option code is used to ask whether, and be notified if, auto-configuration should be disabled on the local subnet. The auto-configure option is an 8-bit number. The code for this option is 116, and its length is 1. This code, along with the IP address assignment, allows a DHCP client to determine whether or not it should generate a link-local IP address.

The option takes two values. DoNotAutoConfigure is 0 and AutoConfigure is 1. When a server responds with the value AutoConfigure, the client MAY generate a link-local IP address if appropriate. However, if the server responds with DoNotAutoConfigure, the client MUST NOT generate a link-local IP address, possibly leaving it with no IP address.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is one byte long and holds one of two values: carry on and pick an address if you need to, or do not pick an address. The value zero means the second.

sections.title: What the Client Does
sections.content:
Clients that have auto-configuration capabilities MUST add the Auto-Configure option to the list of options included in its initial DHCPDISCOVER message, and at this time the option's value should be set to AutoConfigure.

When a DHCPOFFER is received it is handled as described in the DHCP specification, with one exception. If the yiaddr field is 0x00000000, the Auto-Configure option must be consulted. If the option is set to AutoConfigure, then the DHCPOFFER MUST be ignored, and the client MAY generate a link-local IP address. If the option is set to DoNotAutoConfigure, the DHCPOFFER MUST be ignored and the client MUST NOT generate a link-local IP address.

If a DHCP client receives any DHCPOFFER which contains a yiaddr of 0x00000000, and the Auto-Configure flag says DoNotAutoConfigure, in the absence of a DHCPOFFER with a valid yiaddr the client MUST NOT generate a link-local IP address. The amount of time a client waits to collect any other DHCPOFFERs is implementation dependent.

DHCPOFFERs with a yiaddr of 0x00000000 will only be sent by DHCP servers supporting the Auto-Configure option when the DHCPDISCOVER contained the Auto-Configure option. Since the DHCPDISCOVER will only contain the Auto-Configure option when a DHCP client knows how to handle it, there will be no interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks the question as part of its first broadcast. If the answer comes back saying do not auto-configure, the client drops the offer and does not invent an address for itself.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
When a DHCP server receives a DHCPDISCOVER it MUST be processed as described in the DHCP specification. However, if no address is chosen for the host, a few additional steps MUST be taken.

If the DHCPDISCOVER does not contain the Auto-Configure option, it is not answered. If the DHCPDISCOVER contains the Auto-Configure option and the site administrator has specified that auto-configuration should be disabled on the subnet the DHCPDISCOVER is originating from, or for the client originating the request, then a DHCPOFFER MUST be sent to the DHCP client. This offer MUST be for the address 0x00000000, and the Auto-Configure option MUST be set to DoNotAutoConfigure. If the site administrator allows auto-configuration on the originating subnet, the DHCPDISCOVER is not answered as before.
sections.plainLanguage: The server only answers this kind of request if the client asked the question and the administrator has asked for it. The answer it gives is an offer of the all-zero address with a flag saying do not pick an address.

sections.title: Mixed Environments and Later Messages
sections.content:
Environments containing a mixture of clients and servers that do and do not support the Auto-Configure option will not be a problem, because every DHCP transaction is between a server and a client.

If a DHCP client sends a request that contains the Auto-Configure tag, a server that does not know what this tag is will respond normally, and according to the DHCP specification the server MUST NOT return a value for that parameter. The server will either respond with a valid DHCPOFFER or not respond at all, and in both cases a client that supports this option will never care what the state of the option is and may auto-configure. If the Auto-Configure option is not present in the DHCPDISCOVER, the server will do nothing about it, and the client will auto-configure if it receives no response and believes that is what it should do. This scenario SHOULD not occur, as any stacks that implement an auto-configuration mechanism MUST implement this option as well.

As this option only affects the initial IP address selection, it does not apply to subsequent DHCP messages. If the client received a lease from a server, future messages such as RENEW, INFORM and ACK have no need to fall over into an auto-configuration state. If the client's lease expires, the client falls back into the INIT state and the initial DHCPDISCOVER is sent as before. A DHCPRELEASE occurs exactly as described in the DHCP specification, and a DHCPDECLINE is sent when the client determines that the address it is trying to use is already in use, so in both cases the state of auto-configuration on the local wire does not matter.
sections.plainLanguage: An old server simply ignores the new option, and an old client never asks, so the two can share a network without trouble. The option only matters at the very start, when the client is choosing an address; once a lease exists, the option is irrelevant.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DHCP per se currently provides no authentication or security mechanisms. Potential exposures to attack are discussed in section 7 of the DHCP protocol specification.

This mechanism does add one other potential attack. Malicious users on a subnet may respond to all DHCP requests with responses telling DHCP clients that they should NOT auto-configure on the local wire. On a network where auto-configuration is required, this will cause all DHCP clients to not choose an address.
sections.plainLanguage: Because DHCP messages are not authenticated, anyone on the same network could answer every request with a message telling clients not to pick an address, which would leave those machines with no address at all.
